quotes.t: Break the chains of your thought, and you break the chains of your body, too.
You are never given a wish without also being given the power to make it true.
Argue for your limitations, and sure enough they are yours.
Our prime purpose in this life is to help others.
The more we care for the happiness of others, the greater is our own sense of well-being.
Do not let the behavior of others destroy your inner peace.
Change the way you look at things and the things you look at change.
Begin to see yourself as a soul with a body rather than a body with a soul.
You cannot always control what goes on outside, but you can always control what goes on inside.
Success comes to those who become success conscious.
The man who does more than he is paid for will soon be paid for more than he does.
Do not wait. The time will never be just right.
It is not that I am so smart, it is just that I stay with problems longer.
Try not to become a person of success, but rather try to become a person of value.
A calm and modest life brings more happiness than the pursuit of success combined with constant restlessness.
Some things are within our power, and some things are not.
Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of them.
Only the educated are free.
Out beyond ideas of wrongdoing and rightdoing there is a field. I will meet you there.
Do not be satisfied with the stories that come before you. Unfold your own myth.
The inspiration you seek is already within you. Be silent and listen.
All the world's a stage, and all the men and women merely players.
Better three hours too soon than a minute too late.
Cowards die many times before their deaths.
The soul becomes dyed with the colour of its thoughts.
Dwell on the beauty of life. Watch the stars, and see yourself running with them.
Look well into thyself; there is a source of strength which will always spring up if thou wilt always look.
You give but little when you give of your possessions. It is when you give of yourself that you truly give.
When you work you are a flute through whose heart the whispering of the hours turns to music.
For life and death are one, even as the river and the sea are one.
Let us be at peace with our bodies and our minds.
Breathe in deeply to bring your mind home to your body.
If we are peaceful, if we are happy, we can smile and blossom like a flower.
Knowing is not enough; we must apply. Willing is not enough; we must do.
Love does not dominate, it cultivates.
In the realm of ideas everything depends on enthusiasm; in the real world all rests on perseverance.
The mountain remains unmoved at its seeming defeat by the mist.
Rest belongs to the work as the eyelids to the eyes.
Every child comes with the message that God is not yet discouraged of man.
The probability that we may fail in the struggle ought not to deter us from the support of a cause we believe to be just.
I do the very best I know how, the very best I can, and I mean to keep on doing so until the end.
We cannot escape history.
Absorb what is useful, discard what is not, add what is uniquely your own.
Do not fear failure. Not failure, but low aim, is the crime. In great attempts it is glorious even to fail.
It is not the daily increase but daily decrease. Hack away at the unessential.
We suffer more in imagination than in reality.
Wherever there is a human being, there is an opportunity for a kindness.
As is a tale, so is life: not how long it is, but how good it is, that matters.
All men by nature desire to know.
A friend to all is a friend to none.
Happiness is the meaning and the purpose of life, the whole aim and end of human existence.
Do something every day that you do not want to do; this is the golden rule for acquiring the habit of doing your duty without pain.
It is curious that physical courage should be so common in the world and moral courage so rare.
If you tell the truth, you do not have to remember anything.
If you do what you have always done, you will get what you have always gotten.
Change happens when the pain of staying the same is greater than the pain of change.
Success is doing what you want, when you want, where you want, with whom you want, as much as you want.
The privilege of a lifetime is to become who you truly are.
We cannot change anything unless we accept it. Condemnation does not liberate, it oppresses.
The meeting of two personalities is like the contact of two chemical substances; if there is any reaction, both are transformed.
Freedom is not worth having if it does not connote freedom to err.
In war, then, let your great object be victory, not lengthy campaigns.
Do not regret what you have done.
Life imitates art far more than art imitates life.
If we open a quarrel between the past and the present, we shall find that we have lost the future.
But still, like air, I'll rise.
Knowledge is love and light and vision.
We are responsible for what we are, and whatever we wish ourselves to be, we have the power to make ourselves.
Surround yourself with only people who are going to lift you higher.
Don't read success stories, you will only get a message. Read failure stories, you will get some ideas to get success.
The greatest disease in the West today is not TB or leprosy; it is being unwanted, unloved, and uncared for.
Man is only a reed, the weakest in nature, but he is a thinking reed.
When you cease to make a contribution, you begin to die.
The palace is not safe when the cottage is not happy.
Art washes away from the soul the dust of everyday life.
The noblest pleasure is the joy of understanding.
Part of being optimistic is keeping one's head pointed toward the sun, one's feet moving forward.
All you need is love.
He who can, does. He who cannot, teaches.
Adversity makes men, and prosperity makes monsters.
What is a rebel? A man who says no.
Become who you are.
Knowledge must come through action.
Example is not the main thing in influencing others. It is the only thing.
A leader is a dealer in hope.
To will oneself moral and to will oneself free are one and the same decision.
I do not wish women to have power over men, but over themselves.
The worth of a State, in the long run, is the worth of the individuals composing it.
To be without some of the things you want is an indispensable part of happiness.
Life, like a dome of many-coloured glass, stains the white radiance of Eternity.
We shall find peace. We shall hear angels, we shall see the sky sparkling with diamonds.
Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard are sweeter.
I celebrate myself, and sing myself.
If I can stop one heart from breaking, I shall not live in vain.
For most of history, Anonymous was a woman.
The person, be it gentleman or lady, who has not pleasure in a good novel, must be intolerably stupid.
Man only likes to count his troubles; he doesn't calculate his happiness.
All, everything that I understand, I understand only because I love.
We need never be ashamed of our tears.
I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately.

A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.bio: Indian aerospace scientist and the 11th President of India (2002-2007), known as the 'Missile Man of India'.

Abraham Lincoln.bio: 16th president of the United States (1861-1865), who led the country through the Civil War and abolished slavery.

Albert Camus.bio: French-Algerian writer and philosopher, author of The Stranger; Nobel Prize in Literature 1957.

Albert Einstein.bio: German-born theoretical physicist who developed the theory of relativity, one of the pillars of modern physics. He won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for his explanation of the photoelectric effect.
Albert Einstein.credit: Photograph by Orren Jack Turner, Princeton, N.J. Modified with Photoshop by PM_Poon and later by Dantadd., Public domain (File: Albert Einstein Head.jpg)

Albert Schweitzer.bio: Albert Schweitzer was an Alsatian theologian, musician and physician who founded a hospital at Lambaréné in Gabon and served there for decades. His philosophy of reverence for life and his Bach scholarship earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1952.

Anton Chekhov.bio: Anton Chekhov was a Russian playwright and master of the short story, a practising doctor who wrote The Cherry Orchard, Uncle Vanya and hundreds of stories. His restrained, humane art reshaped both the theatre and short fiction of the 20th century.

Aristotle.bio: Greek philosopher and student of Plato; founder of logic and many scientific fields.

Benjamin Disraeli.bio: British statesman who served twice as Prime Minister and led the Conservative Party. He was also a successful novelist, writing books such as Coningsby and Sybil.
Benjamin Disraeli.credit: Cornelius Jabez Hughes, Public domain (File: File:Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield.jpg)

Bertrand Russell.bio: British philosopher, logician and social critic, co-author of Principia Mathematica. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1950 and wrote the popular History of Western Philosophy.

Blaise Pascal.bio: French mathematician, physicist and philosopher, author of the Pensées.
Blaise Pascal.credit: unknown; a copy of the painting of François II Quesnel, which was made for Gérard Edelinck en 1691, Public domain

Bruce Lee.bio: Bruce Lee was a Hong Kong-American martial artist and actor who transformed martial-arts cinema with films such as Enter the Dragon. His philosophy of adaptability — 'be water' — blended Taoist ideas with his own Jeet Kune Do.
Bruce Lee.credit: National General Pictures, Public domain (File: File:Bruce Lee 1971 National General Pictures publicity photo.jpg)

Carl Jung.bio: Swiss psychiatrist who founded analytical psychology. His concepts of the collective unconscious, archetypes and introversion and extraversion remain influential in psychology and culture.
Carl Jung.credit: AnonymousUnknown author, Public domain (File: File:CARL JUNG (1875 - 1961).jpg)

Charles Dickens.bio: English novelist and social critic; author of A Christmas Carol, Oliver Twist and Great Expectations.

Dalai Lama.bio: The 14th Dalai Lama, spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism; Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1989), based in Dharamshala, India.

Eleanor Roosevelt.bio: Eleanor Roosevelt was the longest-serving First Lady of the United States, from 1933 to 1945, and reinvented the role as a platform for civil rights and social reform. Afterward she became a US delegate to the United Nations and chaired the commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
Eleanor Roosevelt.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author, Public domain (File: Eleanor Roosevelt portrait 1933.jpg)

Emily Dickinson.bio: American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems, mostly unpublished in her lifetime, made her a central figure of American literature.
Emily Dickinson.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain

Epictetus.bio: Epictetus was a Greek-born slave in Rome who won his freedom and became one of the most influential Stoic teachers. His Discourses and the handbook known as the Enchiridion teach that freedom lies in mastering one's own judgments and desires.

Friedrich Nietzsche.bio: German philosopher known for Thus Spoke Zarathustra and the concept of the will to power.

Fyodor Dostoevsky.bio: Russian novelist, author of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.

George Bernard Shaw.bio: Irish playwright and critic; author of Pygmalion; Nobel Prize in Literature 1925.
George Bernard Shaw.credit: Sussman, Public domain (File: George Bernard Shaw, playwright (SAYRE 9001).jpg)

Helen Keller.bio: American author and activist who, deaf and blind from childhood, became a renowned advocate for disability rights.
Helen Keller.credit: Los Angeles Times; restored by User:Rhododendrites, Public domain

Henry David Thoreau.bio: American writer known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience.

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.bio: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was a German writer, poet, playwright and natural philosopher, regarded as Germany's greatest literary figure. His works include the drama Faust, The Sorrows of Young Werther and Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship.
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.credit: Joseph Karl Stieler, Public domain (File: Goethe (Stieler 1828).jpg)

John Keats.bio: English Romantic poet of the great Odes, including Ode to a Nightingale.

John Lennon.bio: English singer-songwriter, co-founder of the Beatles and solo artist known for Imagine.

John Stuart Mill.bio: John Stuart Mill was an English philosopher and political economist, the most influential liberal thinker of the 19th century. On Liberty defended individual freedom against social coercion, and his Autobiography candidly records his extraordinary education and mental crisis.

Kahlil Gibran.bio: Lebanese-American writer and poet, best known for The Prophet (1923), one of the best-selling books of all time.

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Leonardo da Vinci.bio: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian Renaissance painter, engineer and anatomist whose notebooks reveal an insatiable curiosity about nature and art. He painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, and filled thousands of pages with studies, inventions and observations.
Leonardo da Vinci.credit: Leonardo da Vinci, Public domain (File: Leonardo self.jpg)

Mahatma Gandhi.bio: Leader of India's nonviolent independence movement; pioneered satyagraha and became the father of the Indian nation.

Marcus Aurelius.bio: Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher, author of the Meditations.

Mark Twain.bio: American writer (Samuel Clemens) known for Adventures of Huckleberry Finn and The Adventures of Tom Sawyer.

Mary Wollstonecraft.bio: Mary Wollstonecraft was an English writer and advocate of women's rights, best known for A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792). She argued that women are not naturally inferior to men but appear so because of a lack of education. She was the mother of Frankenstein author Mary Shelley.

Maya Angelou.bio: American poet and memoirist best known for I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969).
Maya Angelou.credit: Bee Photos by Ryan Marty, Public domain

Miyamoto Musashi.bio: Legendary Japanese swordsman, undefeated in over sixty duels, author of The Book of Five Rings and the Dokkodo.

Mother Teresa.bio: Albanian-Indian Catholic nun who founded the Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata; Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1979).
Mother Teresa.credit: John Mathew Smith & www.celebrity-photos.com from Laurel  Maryland, USA, CC BY-SA 2.0

Napoleon Bonaparte.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French in 1804. His Napoleonic Wars reshaped Europe, and his Napoleonic Code influenced legal systems worldwide. He died in exile on Saint Helena.

Napoleon Hill.bio: Napoleon Hill was an American self-help author best known for Think and Grow Rich (1937), one of the best-selling books of its kind. His work popularized the idea that success follows from definite purpose and a positive mental attitude.
Napoleon Hill.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author, Public domain (File: Napoleon Hill headshot.jpg)

Nelson Mandela.role: Anti-apartheid leader, President of South Africa
Nelson Mandela.bio: South African anti-apartheid revolutionary who spent 27 years in prison and became the country's first Black president in 1994.

Oprah Winfrey.bio: American talk-show host and media executive whose long-running show made her one of the most influential broadcasters in history.
Oprah Winfrey.credit: US Embassy South Africa, Public domain

Oscar Wilde.bio: Irish playwright, poet and author of The Picture of Dorian Gray, famed for his wit and epigrams.
Oscar Wilde.credit: Napoleon Sarony (restoration by Adam Cuerden), Public domain

Pablo Picasso.bio: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist who co-founded Cubism and reinvented his style across a career of nearly eighty years. Works such as Les Demoiselles d'Avignon and Guernica made him the most famous and influential artist of the 20th century.
Pablo Picasso.credit: Didier Descouens, Public domain (File: File:(Barcelona) Retrat de Picasso - Pablo Gargallo - Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya.jpg)

Percy Shelley.bio: Percy Bysshe Shelley was an English Romantic poet known for lyrics such as 'Ozymandias', 'Ode to the West Wind' and Adonais. He was married to Mary Shelley, author of Frankenstein.

Rabindranath Tagore.bio: Bengali poet and polymath from India; the first non-European Nobel laureate in Literature (1913), known for Gitanjali.

Richard Bach.bio: Richard Bach is an American writer best known for the bestselling novella Jonathan Livingston Seagull (1970) and Illusions (1977). A former Air Force pilot, his work often combines flying with spiritual themes.
Richard Bach.credit: Corsair133693, CC BY-SA 3.0 (File: File:Von Richthofen LYNN GARRISON - DICK BACH.jpg)

Rumi.bio: 13th-century Persian poet and Sufi mystic whose Masnavi is among the most influential works of Islamic literature.

Seneca.bio: Roman Stoic philosopher and statesman, author of Letters to Lucilius.

Simone de Beauvoir.bio: French writer and existentialist philosopher, author of The Second Sex.

Sophocles.bio: Sophocles was an Athenian tragedian who wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete. Oedipus Rex and Antigone, his most famous works, set the pattern for Western tragedy.

Sun Tzu.bio: Ancient Chinese general traditionally credited with The Art of War, a treatise on strategy studied worldwide for over two thousand years.
Sun Tzu.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: 吴司马孙武.jpg)

Swami Vivekananda.bio: Indian Hindu monk who introduced Vedanta and Yoga to the West; famous for his 1893 Chicago Parliament of Religions address.
Swami Vivekananda.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: Swami Vivekananda at Parliament of Religions.jpg)

Thich Nhat Hanh.bio: Vietnamese Buddhist monk and peace activist who popularized mindfulness in the West; nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize by Martin Luther King Jr.
Thich Nhat Hanh.credit: CC BY-SA 4.0 (File: File:Hòa thượng Ấn Kim - Tổ Tuân - Hoằng Tịnh. 印 金 祖 恂 弘 净.jpg)

Tony Robbins.bio: Tony Robbins is an American author, coach and motivational speaker known for bestselling books such as Unlimited Power and Awaken the Giant Within. His seminars and self-help programmes have made him one of the most prominent figures in the personal development industry.

Victor Hugo.bio: French poet and novelist, author of Les Misérables and The Hunchback of Notre-Dame.
Victor Hugo.credit: Étienne Carjat, Public domain (File: Victor Hugo by Étienne Carjat 1876 - full.jpg)

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Walt Whitman.bio: American poet best known for the collection Leaves of Grass (1855).

Wayne Dyer.bio: Wayne Dyer was an American self-help author and motivational speaker whose first book, Your Erroneous Zones (1976), became one of the best-selling books of all time. He wrote more than forty books and lectured widely on self-development and spirituality.

William Shakespeare.bio: English playwright and poet, widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language; author of Hamlet and Macbeth.

Winston Churchill.bio: British prime minister during the Second World War and Nobel laureate in Literature.
